title: Why can't you tickle yourself?
hook: Try it right now: tickle your own ribs. Nothing, right? But when someone else does it, you can't stop laughing. Why can't you tickle yourself?
notes: Claims follow the research pack: Wikipedia 'Tickling' (Self-tickling section: surprise, Blakemore and colleagues 1998, joystick-controlled tickling robot, cerebellum informs the somatosensory cortex, an unknown cortical mechanism decreases the sensation) and Wikipedia 'Efference copy' (efference copy of motor commands; a delay between the self-produced command and the robot's touch increases perceived tickliness; matching predicted and actual feedback is attenuated).
The only number is 1998, stated in the Tickling article.

beats.narration: Try it right now: tickle your own ribs. Nothing, right? But when someone else does it, you can't stop laughing. Why can't you tickle yourself?
Same hand movement, same skin. The difference isn't in your skin at all. It's a prediction your brain makes before you even move.
Every time you move, your brain sends a command to your muscles. And it keeps a copy of that command, called an efference copy.
Your cerebellum uses that copy to predict exactly what you'll feel, and where. When the touch arrives right on schedule, your brain turns the feeling down.
Here's the twist. In 1998, scientists had people tickle themselves through a robot they steered with a joystick. They still couldn't make themselves laugh.
But when the robot's touch came with a delay, the prediction stopped matching, and the touch felt far more tickly.
Tickling needs surprise. And your brain can't surprise itself, so it cancels the tickle before it lands.
So why can't you tickle yourself? Because your brain always sees it coming. Stay curious!
